Q: Running a Class.method() when that module is imported A:

You can make a decorator do what you want:

def onLoad(cls):
    cls.onLoad(cls)
    return cls

@onLoad
class Class1():
    var1 = 0

    def onLoad(cls):
        cls.var1 = 1
 

print(f"{Class1.var1 = }")

This code will call the method you want on the first time this is imported into your project.

You probably meant to use a @classmethod:

def onLoad(cls):
    cls.onLoad()
    return cls

@onLoad
class Class1():
    var1 = 0

    @classmethod
    def onLoad(cls):
        cls.var1 = 1
 

print(f"{Class1.var1 = }")

Q: New Turing Omnibus Time and Complexity Chapter A:

To apply the Gauss formula, all elements need to be equally spaced. To do this, you need to "extend" the last value:

4 = 3(1) + 1 + 3(0)

the sum become:

1 + 3(n - 1) + 1 + 3(n - 2) ... 1 + 3(2) + 1 + 3(1) + 1 + 3(0)

Now we can apply the formula:

(1 + 3(0) + 1 + 3(n - 1) ) * n /2

Wich give us:

n + 3(n - 1)n/2

With the book formula, making the inverse proccess we have:

n + 1 + 3n(n - 1)/2 = n(1 + 2/n + 1 + 3(n-1) )/2

So, with this formula it is necessary that the first element will be 2/n. Maybe the book is talking about large n, so 2/n goes to zero?

Q: how to use an MS-Access file from Linux? A:

I ran into this problem myself a few years ago. I needed to work with an existing Microsoft Access database from Linux, and getting the connection working was surprisingly painful. I eventually got UCanAccess + JDBC working, but it involved manually dealing with Java, JARs, dependencies, and the classpath.

I recently came back to the problem and decided to package what I learned into a small open-source project:

mdb-bridge

It provides a Python API for connecting to .mdb / .accdb files from Linux using:

Python → JayDeBeApi → JDBC → UCanAccess → Access

The goal is to make the setup less painful: the project uses uv for the Python environment and Maven to manage the Java/UCanAccess dependencies, rather than requiring you to manually download the JARs and build the classpath yourself.

Once connected, you can execute SQL against the Access database through the Python API. For example:

from access_tool.connection import AccessConnection

connection = AccessConnection("database.mdb").connect()

rows = connection.execute("SELECT * FROM my_table")

connection.close()

I tested the current setup on Ubuntu/WSL2 with Java 17 in August 2026.

It's still a small project and I'm continuing to build it out, but I thought I'd share it here since this question is exactly the kind of problem that led me to build it in the first place. Hopefully it saves someone else from having to fight with the setup as much as I did.

Q: PDF Compression Techniques A:

PDFs are already compressed in a number of ways, which prevents the external compression utilities from gaining much ground. It should be obvious that if you unpack the PDF, then the external utilities would have an easier time finding redundancies and patterns to compress.

I know of no tool to unpack the PDF without reprinting it though. Ghostscript can reprint the exiting PDF into a new PDF, and we can tell it to avoid compression in that second version.

gs -dCompressPages=false -dCompressFonts=false -dCompressStreams=false -dEncodeColorImages=false -dEncodeGrayImages=false -dEncodeMonoImages=false -dNOPAUSE -dBATCH -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dPDFSETTINGS=/screen -dSubsetFonts=true -dColorImageResolution=96 -dGrayImageResolution=96 -sOutputFile=raw-copy.pdf src.pdf

Even though the resulting copy is large (as it uses no compression), it can be more effectively packed with external tools

zpaq a raw-copy.pdf.zpaq raw-copy.pdf -m56,25,3 -fragment 9
zstd --ultra -22 raw-copy.pdf

A useful side effect is that we can compress together different versions of a text (unpacked PDFs, unpacked EPUBs, HTMLs, DOCs, RTFs and so on), eliminating redundancy and saving storage space across formats.

p.s. Sometimes the modified https://github.com/kaitz/zpaqf is better than the original in compressing PDFs, it depends on the PDF.

p.s. Even better are https://github.com/hxim/paq8px and https://github.com/schnaader/precomp-cpp, as they transparently repack some of the underlying compression.
